video_title: The Energy Supercycle Could Last Into the 2030s | Josef Schachter
gist: Calgary energy analyst Josef Schachter argues the post-2020 energy and commodity cycle is structural and will last into the 2030s, forecasting $80 WTI for 2026, $90 for 2027 and a spike above $150 before 2030. He sees cheap North American producers (about 2.7-3.7x cash flow versus 7-13 years PDP), services and gas names as bargains, with infrastructure delays and critical-mineral build-outs extending the cycle.

themes.theme: Energy supercycle thesis and historical analogs

insights.claim: Schachter argues the current energy and broader commodity upcycle began after COVID in 2020 and will last into the 2030s, driven by underinvestment followed by demand and a supply shock.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Frames energy equities as a multi-year investing market rather than a short trade.
insights.quote: I think this cycle started in 2020 after co and I think it's going to last into the 2030s.

insights.claim: He maps prior regimes: 1974-81 was an investing market (stocks up 15x) ended by Volcker's 21% rates; 1981-1999 was a trading market; China's opening after 1999 lifted oil from $10 to $147 in summer 2008.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Uses investing-vs-trading market regimes to judge when to hold versus trade energy stocks.

insights.claim: China's import need rose from about 0.5 mb/d to roughly 10 mb/d between the 1990s and 1999 as consumption hit 14 mb/d against 4 mb/d production, which he credits as the marginal driver of the 1999-2008 oil rally.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: The current cycle lacks one single demand driver like China, so its drivers are more diffuse and supply-side.

insights.claim: Energy bull markets are not straight lines: WTI saw five corrections of 20-40% between 1999 and 2008, so he expects sharp pullbacks inside this cycle too.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Expect to be offered dips; position sizing should tolerate 20-40% drawdowns.
insights.quote: Just pull out WTI from 99 to 08. There were five major corrections between 20 and 40%.

themes.theme: Oil price forecasts and supply-demand balance

insights.claim: His company forecasts use $80 WTI for 2026 (possibly 84-85 given early Q3 reporters) and $90 WTI for 2027, with WTI near 102 and Brent near 107 at recording.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Gives explicit price decks to test against current equity valuations.

insights.claim: He predicts WTI will exceed $150 before the end of this decade and could reach 200-plus in the 2030s via a supply disruption, citing 2008 when WTI went from 90 to 147 in under six months.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Supports owning convex upside exposure to oil, but the call is an explicit tail scenario.
insights.quote: I think before the end of this decade we're going to be over the 150.

insights.claim: OECD demand is expected to fall 2-3 million bpd by 2035 while non-OECD demand grows by more than 10 million bpd, taking global demand from about 105 to 115 million bpd by the 2030s.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Demand growth is an emerging-market story, so watch non-OECD data over US data.

insights.claim: The 2025 demand increase of about 300,000 bpd (105.3 vs 105 million) came entirely from the United States per weekly EIA data, and the 20-year average growth ex-COVID/war/recession is 1.2 million bpd, versus an OPEC forecast of 2 million for 2027 that assumes the war ends.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: OPEC's 2027 demand forecast embeds a peace assumption that Schachter does not share.

insights.claim: Marginal supply must come from expensive deepwater and difficult regions (Namibia, offshore Africa, Brazil, Guyana), so oil must stay high long enough to justify capex: the world has run out of $2 oil in the 1970s, $10 in the 1990s and is now running out of $50-70 oil.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: A rising marginal cost floor argues against a return to $50-70 oil.
insights.quote: We're now running out of 50 and $70 oil

insights.claim: Even if the war ends and OPEC opens up, he allows WTI could return to $70, but SPR refills and rebuilding of destroyed Middle East pipelines, refineries and chemical plants would support prices.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Peace is not automatically bearish; restocking and rebuild demand cushions the downside.

insights.claim: Infrastructure delays (TMX pipeline over budget, long permitting, environmental and First Nations processes) lengthen the cycle by slowing supply response.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Slow supply response is the mechanism that extends price strength.

themes.theme: Equity valuation and where the bargains are

insights.claim: Energy producers trade at 2-3x depressed cash flow at cycle bottoms and 8-10x peak cash flow at tops, so multiple expansion plus higher reserve values should amplify returns as prices rise.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Valuation upside comes from both cash flow growth and multiple re-rating.

insights.claim: He screens for low cash-flow multiple versus proved-developed-producing (PDP) reserve life, citing names at 2.7x cash flow with 7.2 years PDP, 3.7x with 12.7, 3.2x with 6.7, and says bargains remain.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Cash-flow multiple versus PDP life is a practical screen for Canadian producers.
insights.quote: So there are bargains still available.

insights.claim: Producers currently prioritize debt paydown, normal course issuer bid buybacks and dividends, and will not issue equity until shares reach roughly 7x cash flow, with growth becoming a bigger component later in the cycle.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Capital discipline supports free cash flow now; a shift to growth capex and equity issuance would signal late-cycle.

insights.claim: Service companies (drillers, frackers) in the US and Canada look cheap and should post better quarterly results, and gas-weighted stocks are cheaper than oily names because gas has lagged.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Services and gas equities are higher-beta ways to play the cycle if prices improve.

insights.claim: North American producers should trade at a premium because the US (22-23 million bpd) and Canada (6.1 million bpd) have long reserve life, easy transport and security of supply, and international majors who sold assets may return later in the cycle.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Supply security premium favors North American reserves over foreign assets.

insights.claim: LNG Canada currently runs about 2 bcf/d and, with approvals and First Nations support, Canadian LNG capacity could reach 6-7 bcf/d by the early 2030s from nothing two years ago; a sustained NYMEX gas price of 5-6 would transform gas producer cash flows.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Canadian gas and LNG-linked infrastructure is a lagging leg of the cycle.

insights.claim: Associated gas constrains oil growth, as in New Mexico where operators paid multi-million dollars per well opportunity once two new pipelines allowed gas takeaway.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Midstream takeaway capacity unlocks upstream value.

insights.claim: A roughly 1 million bpd TMX expansion to the West Coast is being discussed with federal and provincial support, with Pembina involved and 10% First Nations ownership; he expects Canada to lose 1-2 million bpd of US market share over the decade, hence the need for coastal access.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Pipeline owners benefit from Canadian diversification away from the US market.

themes.theme: Critical minerals, power and data centers

insights.claim: The demand driver this cycle is raw materials for the build-out (copper, aluminum, nickel, lithium, uranium) sourced from Africa, South America and Asia, creating a large capital cycle; data centers face shortages of copper and power.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Commodity bulls are linked to AI infrastructure through physical bottlenecks.

insights.claim: He sees data center projects slowing due to power, water and input constraints and community backlash, blaming developer hubris for ignoring higher power rates and the lack of tax revenue for 20 years.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Social license risk is a headwind for AI build-out timelines and a tailwind for scarce inputs.

insights.claim: Export controls are a risk: diesel export limits would backfire because refiners cannot cut diesel without cutting jet fuel and gasoline, while a more likely risk is China restricting critical mineral exports.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Critical minerals export controls are likelier than fuel export bans.
insights.quote: The key thing is going to be in the next few years as America starts to have enough of these critical minerals

insights.claim: OPEC remains the swing producer with the most upside: Saudi Arabia could return to 12-13 million bpd from about 8, Russia to 12-13 from about 8, and Iraq could double production over the decade.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Large latent OPEC capacity is the main bear risk if geopolitics normalize.

insights.claim: Venezuela produces about 1.3 million bpd; reaching 3-3.5 million requires rebuilding destroyed facilities, repairing rusted pipelines and cleaning Orinoco environmental damage, with Chevron the key US participant.
insights.speaker: Josef Schachter
insights.so_what: Venezuelan upside is slow and capex heavy, not a near-term supply flood.
